vulnerabilities.title: MPROTECT_PERMISSION_LOGIC_FLAW

root_cause.description: main calls mprotect(buf, 0x64, 4) where 4 = PROT_READ only. This removes both write (W) and execute (X) permissions from the shellcode buffer. The subsequent 'jmp rdi' at 0x149a jumps to a non-executable page. Under NX (enabled per S1), this causes SIGSEGV. The intended value was almost certainly PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC = 5, which would remove write permission while keeping the region executable. The hardcoded value 4 instead of 5 is a logic error in the permission argument construction.

affected_objects: mmap buffer at 0x13370000 (100 bytes, RWX -> R after mprotect)

attack_surface.input: shellcode via read(0, buf, 0x63) from stdin
data_flow: stdin -> read(0, buf, 0x63) at 0x13dc writes up to 99 bytes into mmap buffer at 0x13370000
mprotect(buf, 0x64, 4) at 0x1429 changes region from RWX to PROT_READ (R-only)
registers cleared: rax-r15, rsp, rbp, xmm0-xmm15 all zeroed at 0x142e-0x1492
jmp rdi at 0x149a transfers control to non-executable shellcode buffer

security_check.expected: mprotect should be called with PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC (5) to make the shellcode buffer executable (read+execute) while removing write permission, preventing self-modifying code while allowing execution
security_check.actual: mprotect is called with PROT_READ (4), making the buffer read-only and non-executable. The jmp rdi at 0x149a targets a page without execute permission.
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: The permission argument is 4 (PROT_READ) instead of 5 (PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC). This is an incorrect constant value in the mprotect call, not a missing check.

vulnerable_operation.expression: mprotect(buf, 0x64, 4); ... jmp rdi  [where rdi=0x13370000, buf is now PROT_READ only]

impact.reason: The jmp rdi at 0x149a transfers control to a PROT_READ (non-executable) page. With NX enabled (GNU_STACK=RW, confirmed by S1), the CPU will raise a SIGSEGV when attempting to execute instructions from a non-executable page. S1's probe_io with input 'AAAA' (no 0x0f byte) confirmed a Segmentation fault, consistent with this analysis. Any shellcode input that passes the blacklist check will result in SIGSEGV at the jmp.

Since the shellcode buffer is non-executable after mprotect(buf, 0x64, 4), no user-supplied shellcode can ever execute. The program always crashes with SIGSEGV on the jmp. This constitutes a denial-of-service condition: the shellcode execution feature is completely broken.

evidence.description: Disassembly at 0x141c: mov edx, 0x4; mov esi, 0x64; mov rdi, rax; call mprotect@plt. The third argument (edx) is 0x4 = PROT_READ, not 0x5 = PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC. This removes execute permission from the shellcode buffer.

Disassembly at 0x149a: jmp rdi. At this point rdi=0x13370000 (set at 0x1493 from [rbp-0x18]). The target page has PROT_READ only (no execute) due to the mprotect at 0x1429. Under NX, this causes SIGSEGV.

The mmap at 0x1382 is called with edx=0x7 (PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE|PROT_EXEC = RWX). The buffer starts as RWX, but mprotect at 0x1429 downgrades it to PROT_READ (4), removing both W and X. The intent was likely to remove only W (value 5), keeping X for execution.

S1 fact F012 confirms: probe_io with input 'AAAA' (no 0x0f byte, passes blacklist) resulted in Segmentation fault. This is consistent with jmp to a non-executable PROT_READ page under NX. The crash occurs regardless of shellcode content, proving the mprotect permission value is the root cause.

verification_required: Confirm at runtime that the SIGSEGV is specifically due to non-executable page (NX violation) and not another cause
Confirm whether mprotect(buf, 0x64, 5) would allow shellcode execution if the value were corrected

vulnerabilities.title: MPROTECT_RETURN_VALUE_UNCHECKED

root_cause.description: main calls mprotect(buf, 0x64, 4) at 0x1429 but does not check the return value. mprotect returns 0 on success and -1 on failure. If mprotect fails (e.g., due to an invalid argument, permission issue, or other error), the mmap buffer retains its original RWX permissions. The code proceeds directly to clear registers and jmp rdi, executing shellcode from an RWX region. This is a missing security check on a critical permission-changing operation.

affected_objects: mmap buffer at 0x13370000 (100 bytes, RWX if mprotect fails)

attack_surface.input: shellcode via read(0, buf, 0x63) from stdin
data_flow: read(0, buf, 0x63) writes user shellcode into RWX buffer
mprotect(buf, 0x64, 4) at 0x1429 — return value NOT checked
If mprotect fails: buffer remains RWX, shellcode is executable
jmp rdi at 0x149a executes shellcode from RWX buffer

security_check.expected: After calling mprotect, the code should check the return value. If mprotect returns -1 (failure), the program should abort or handle the error, because the buffer would retain RWX permissions and shellcode would be executable.
security_check.actual: The return value of mprotect is completely ignored. After 'call mprotect@plt' at 0x1429, the code immediately proceeds to clear registers (0x142e) and jmp rdi (0x149a) without any conditional branch on the mprotect result.
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: Missing return value check for mprotect. Compare with mmap at 0x138b-0x1390 where the return IS checked against -1, and read at 0x13e4-0x13e8 where the return IS checked against 0. The mprotect call has no equivalent check.

vulnerable_operation.address: 0x1429 (mprotect call, no check follows) and 0x149a (jmp rdi)
vulnerable_operation.expression:
mprotect(buf, 0x64, 4);  // no check on return value
... jmp rdi  // if mprotect failed, buf is still RWX

impact.reason: If mprotect fails, the mmap buffer retains RWX permissions. The jmp rdi at 0x149a would then execute user-supplied shellcode from an RWX region. The shellcode could perform arbitrary memory operations (read/write) within the process address space. This is a theoretical impact because mprotect failure is not guaranteed — it depends on runtime conditions (kernel, permissions, address validity). Under normal conditions with a valid mmap buffer, mprotect(buf, 0x64, 4) should succeed.

evidence.description: Disassembly: at 0x1429 'call mprotect@plt', immediately followed at 0x142e by 'xor rax,rax' (start of register clearing). There is no 'cmp eax, 0xffffffff' or 'test eax,eax' or any conditional jump between the mprotect call and the register clearing. The return value is discarded.

Contrast with mmap handling: at 0x138b 'cmp QWORD PTR [rbp-0x10], 0xffffffffffffffff' followed by 'jne' — mmap return IS checked. And read at 0x13e4 'cmp DWORD PTR [rbp-0x1c], 0x0' followed by 'jne' — read return IS checked. But mprotect at 0x1429 has NO such check, establishing the pattern that return value checking is expected but missing for mprotect.

verification_required: Determine if there are runtime conditions under which mprotect(buf, 0x64, 4) would fail for a valid mmap buffer at a fixed address
If mprotect can fail, verify that the buffer retains RWX permissions and shellcode executes

vulnerabilities.title: BLACKLIST_INCOMPLETE_FILTER

root_cause.description: The blacklist function only checks for byte 0x0f (the first byte of the x86-64 syscall instruction 0f 05). This is the sole filter on user-supplied shellcode. The filter is incomplete: (1) it does not block the 'int 0x80' instruction (CD 80), which is an alternative syscall mechanism on x86-64; (2) it does not block other 0x0f-prefixed two-byte instructions that could be used to construct syscall indirectly; (3) if the mprotect logic flaw (BUG-001) were corrected to PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC (5), the shellcode would be executable and the blacklist would be the only defense — but it only blocks one specific byte value, leaving numerous bypass paths.

attack_surface.input: shellcode bytes via read(0, buf, 0x63) from stdin
data_flow: read(0, buf, 0x63) writes user shellcode into mmap buffer
blacklist(buf) at 0x1400 iterates i=0..99, checks if buf[i] == 0x0f
If no byte == 0x0f: return 0 -> continue to mprotect and jmp

security_check.expected: If the intent is to prevent syscall-based shellcode, the filter should block all syscall mechanisms: 'syscall' (0f 05), 'int 0x80' (CD 80), and potentially other indirect syscall methods. A single-byte check for 0x0f is insufficient.
security_check.actual: blacklist only checks if any byte equals 0x0f. It does not check for 0xCD (int instruction opcode) or 0x80 (the interrupt number in 'int 0x80'). The 'int 0x80' instruction (bytes CD 80) passes the blacklist entirely.
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: Missing check for 'int 0x80' (CD 80) as an alternative syscall mechanism. The filter only blocks the 'syscall' instruction prefix byte 0x0f, not the 'int 0x80' instruction.

vulnerable_operation.expression: for i in 0..99: if buf[i] == 0x0f then abort  [only checks 0x0f, not 0xCD or 0x80]

impact.reason: The blacklist is the sole security filter on shellcode content. If the mprotect logic flaw (BUG-001) were corrected to make the buffer executable (PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC=5), the blacklist would be the only defense against malicious shellcode. The 'int 0x80' instruction (CD 80) passes the filter, allowing 32-bit syscall invocation. This would bypass the intended 'no syscall' restriction. However, this impact is theoretical because in the current binary, BUG-001 (PROT_READ=4) prevents any shellcode from executing at all.

evidence.description: Disassembly: at 0x1312 'cmp al, 0xf' followed by 0x1314 'jne 131d'. The only comparison is against 0x0f. There is no comparison against 0xCD (int opcode) or 0x80. The loop iterates i=0..99 (0x1321: cmp [rbp-0x4], 0x63; jle) checking each byte only against 0x0f.

The blacklist function checks exactly one byte value (0x0f) across all 100 bytes. The x86-64 'syscall' instruction is 0f 05 — blocking 0x0f prevents 'syscall'. But 'int 0x80' (CD 80) is an alternative syscall mechanism that does not contain 0x0f and passes the filter entirely. Additionally, endbr64 (F3 0F 1E FA) contains 0x0f, so if CET/IBT is enforced, the blacklist creates a paradox: IBT requires endbr64 at indirect branch targets, but endbr64 contains the blacklisted byte 0x0f.

verification_required: If BUG-001 is corrected (mprotect uses PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC=5), verify that 'int 0x80' shellcode passes the blacklist and executes successfully
Determine whether CET/IBT is enforced at runtime, which would create an endbr64 requirement that conflicts with the 0x0f blacklist

non_vulnerabilities.description: init() calls setvbuf on stdin/stdout/stderr with _IONBF (mode 2) and alarm(60).
non_vulnerabilities.reason: setvbuf parameters are correct (stream, NULL buffer, _IONBF=2, size 0). alarm(60) sets a 60-second timeout which is a standard anti-debugging/DoS prevention measure. No user-controlled input reaches these calls. No vulnerability.

non_vulnerabilities.description: _abort(msg) calls printf('%s', msg) then exit(1). The format string is hardcoded '%s' in .rodata at 0x2008, and msg is always a string literal from .rodata (not user-controlled).
non_vulnerabilities.reason: No format string vulnerability: printf uses '%s' format with a hardcoded string literal argument. No user input reaches the format string or its argument. exit(1) terminates cleanly.

non_vulnerabilities.description: mmap return value is checked: at 0x138b 'cmp [rbp-0x10], 0xffffffffffffffff' and 0x1390 'jne 13a1'. If mmap returns -1 (failure), _abort('mmap failed!') is called.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: The mmap return value check is correct and complete. The comparison against -1 (MAP_FAILED) is the standard idiom. No vulnerability in this check.

non_vulnerabilities.description: read return value is checked: at 0x13e4 'cmp [rbp-0x1c], 0x0' and 0x13e8 'jne 13f9'. If read returns 0 (EOF or error), _abort('read failed!') is called.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: The read return value check is present. However, note that read returning a value > 0 but less than 99 is accepted — the shellcode buffer may contain partially-filled data (rest is zeroed by memset). This is not a vulnerability per se, just means shorter shellcode is accepted. The check for <= 0 is adequate for preventing execution of empty shellcode.

non_vulnerabilities.description: main has a stack canary: at 0x133a 'mov rax, fs:0x28' stored at [rbp-0x8], checked at 0x14a1-0x14b0 before return.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: Stack canary is properly implemented. However, note that the canary check at 0x14a1 is unreachable in normal execution because the jmp rdi at 0x149a never returns — control transfers to shellcode (or crashes). The canary only protects if execution somehow returns to main's epilogue, which does not happen in the normal flow.

unresolved.description: Whether CET (IBT/SHSTK) is actually enforced at runtime. The binary has GNU_PROPERTY noting IBT+SHSTK, but enforcement depends on kernel config and CPU support.
unresolved.reason: S1 uncertainty U002 notes this. If IBT is enforced, the jmp rdi at 0x149a requires the target (0x13370000) to begin with endbr64 (F3 0F 1E FA). But endbr64 contains byte 0x0f which is blacklisted, creating an impossible constraint. If IBT is NOT enforced, this is not an issue. Either way, BUG-001 (PROT_READ=4) causes SIGSEGV before IBT matters.
unresolved.required_next_step: Runtime verification of CET enforcement on the target system (check /proc/cpuinfo for shstk/ibt flags and kernel config).

unresolved.description: Whether the mprotect(buf, 0x64, 4) value is an intentional challenge design or a genuine bug. If PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC (5) was intended, the challenge would be to bypass the 0x0f blacklist to execute shellcode. With PROT_READ (4), no shellcode can execute at all.
unresolved.reason: S1 uncertainty U001 notes this. Static analysis cannot determine developer intent. The value 4 is hardcoded in the binary at 0x141c (mov edx, 0x4).
unresolved.required_next_step: Contextual analysis: if this is a CTF challenge, the intended solution path would clarify whether PROT_READ=4 is intentional (perhaps requiring an mprotect failure bypass) or a bug.

unresolved.description: Whether there are runtime seccomp filters or other sandboxing mechanisms restricting syscalls beyond the binary's own blacklist.
unresolved.reason: S1 uncertainty U003 notes no seccomp symbols in the binary, but a parent process or wrapper could install filters. This affects the severity of BUG-003 (blacklist bypass) if shellcode execution were possible.
unresolved.required_next_step: Runtime check for seccomp filters (e.g., examining /proc/self/status for Seccomp field, or running under strace).
